Resting-State fMRI with the new UI

The New-UI is still under development

We are still working on the implementation of the New UI for HALFpipe. Please report any issue you might encounter at halfpipe@fmri.science or on GitHub.

AUTHOR

Written by Clara El Khantour, Lea Waller, Pierre Lune Bellec, Frank Hillary, Ilya Veer, Clara Moreau

Please address questions and comments to halfpipe@fmri.science. You can also join the HALFpipe Mattermost (similar to Slack) using this link.

How to launch the new UI

  • Singularity/Apptainer
  • Docker
  1. Open a terminal session and connect to your HPC (if applicable).
  2. Run an Interactive Job on the cluster (see the note above)
  • Note: If running on a HPC, you need to run an Interactive Job on the cluster. To do this, please refer to your HPC’s documentation. Then load Singularity/Apptainer packages: module load singularity.
  1. Run the Execution Command for your container software.
apptainer run --contain --cleanenv --bind /:/ext halfpipe_1.3.0.sif --use_cluster --tui
Understanding the command line

  • File Location: Ensure the HALFpipe-1.3.0.sif file is in your current working directory or specify its full path.

  • New UI flag: Use the --tui flag to launch HALFpipe with the new UI.

  • Cluster Flag: Use the --use-cluster flag when running the execution command on an HPC.

  1. Open a terminal session via Docker Desktop.
  2. Run the docker command.
docker run --interactive --tty --volume /:/ext halfpipe/halfpipe:1.3.0 --subject-chunks --nipype-n-procs 1 --keep none --tui
  • Note: To access your files more easily, you can bind in the path where the data, working directory and atlases are located.

For example: --volume /home/user/scratch:/home/user/scratch

Adding more CPUs on a local machine

Note 1: The flags --subject-chunks and --nipype-n-procs 1 are optional. While they may slow down the pipeline, they help ensure you don’t exceed your computer’s processing capacity. Use them if you’re concerned about system limitations.

Note 2: On some systems, Docker will restrict the number of CPU cores available to HALFpipe by default. If your computer can handle it, you can allocate more CPUs using the Docker flag --cpus. Refer to your system’s documentation to learn your CPU limitations.

By adding more CPUs, you can add the HALFpipe flag --nipype-n-procs to accelerate the process. For example:

docker run --interactive --tty --cpus=3 --volume /:/ext halfpipe/halfpipe:1.3.0 --nipype-n-procs --subject-chunks --keep none

Pipeline settings

You have now opened the new user interface (UI) of HALFpipe.

This new interface is user-friendly: you can navigate it using your mouse and select different parameters by clicking on them.

We will first specify the pipeline settings and then the Features.

Understanding the Icons

With this new UI, there are different icons you can interact with:

👁️ : To visualize files found

🖌️ : To edit the section

❌ : To delete the section

❎ : Item selected

✖️ : Item not selected

ℹ️ : To get more information about the section

Specify your working directory

  1. Click on Browse.
  2. Indicate the path you want your working directory to be located. This correspond to your output folder.
You can either select an already existing folder, or create a new one.

To create a new directory, simply add its name to the end of the path. If the folder doesn’t exist, a message will appear indicating it wasn’t found and will prompt you to create it. Click ‘Yes’ to proceed and generate the output folder.

  1. After specifying the working directory, click on Input Data in the top navigation bar.

Specify your Data location

Indicate whether or not the data is in BIDS format

  • If in BIDS
  • If not in BIDS
  1. Click on Browse.
  2. Here, simply indicate the path to your BIDS data. Files will be automatically found, this can take a moment. Let Lesion mask set to OFF
  3. Click on General preprocessing settings in the top navigation bar, and go to the next section.
  1. Switch the button to OFF
  2. Under the section T1W-weighted images, click on Browse.
  3. Select the T1W-weighted file of 1 subject.
  4. Delete the unique subject ID and replace it with {subject}. If applicable, do the same with {run} and {session}.
    • As you modify the path, HALFpipe will indicate how many files it has found. Once your path is correct and all subject files are detected, click OK to save the path.
  5. Follow the same logic for the BOLD data and Field maps (if any) sections.
    • Check repetition time values : click on YES (unless the TR is incorrect)
  6. Go to the bottom, and click on Confirm
  7. Click on General preprocessing settings in the top navigation bar, and go to the next section.
Example of path
  • If your data is organized as path/to/T1/subj01/T1.nii.gz - where subj01 can be any ID you have to enter path/to/T1/{subject}/T1.nii.gz.
  • It will then find T1 files for all subjects: path/to/T1/subj01/T1.nii.gz, path/to/T1/subj02/T1.nii.gz etc…

If your files have been successfully imported, you should see the follow message:

Verify files imported

Verify all the files have been properly found. You can do that by looking at the number of file found. You can also click on the 👁️ to see the detail of the file.

General Preprocessing settings

  1. Switch Slice timing to :
    • ON if you know the slice timing details during the acquisition for your data. If unsure, check with the MR physicist/technician or any dataset information.
      • In the following steps you will check the slice order and slice timing values.
      • Check the metadata automatically found. Then click Yes if these are the expected numbers, otherwise No and specify them.
    • OFF otherwise
Important: If on HPC
  • Switch Advanced setting to ON
  • Switch “Generate workflow for running on a cluster” to ON
  1. Click on Features in the top navigation bar, and go to the next section.

Features

Important – Correction to the a/cCompCor Pipeline Description

Up to HALFpipe v1.3.2, Pipeline 1 in the graphical interface is labeled as aCompCor and indeed applies aCompCor (anatomical CompCor) denoising. This differs from the Terminal UI implementation, where Pipeline 1 applies cCompCor (CSF-only CompCor) (see the note in Section 2.2 of the Resting-state fMRI Manual – Terminal UI).

To harmonize the graphical and terminal interfaces, a future release will introduce cCompCor as a separate denoising option in the graphical interface, following the Terminal UI guidelines.

  1. Click on New
  2. We will now run 4 feature types: Seed-based connectivity, Atlas-based connectivity Matrix, ReHo and fALFF. Each of the features will be extracted with three types of confound removal using:
  • Pipeline 1: aCompCor
  • Pipeline 2: Motion parameters with scrubbing
  • Pipeline 3: Pipeline 2 + Global Signal (GSR)
  • Pipeline 4: Motion parameters
  • Pipeline 5: Pipeline 4 + Global Signal (GSR)

1. Seed-based connectivity

  • Select Seed-based connectivity
  • Feature name: Type seedCorr1

General settings

  1. Select task
  • Click on the session(s) or task(s) corresponding to your resting state data.
  1. Seed images
  • Click on Add.
  • Click on Browse to indicate the path.
  • Select the path of one existing seed. Then modify the path with {seed}.nii.gz
  • Check metadata: click on yes. Then verify that all the seeds are selected.
  1. Minimum brain coverage:
  • Set minimum brain coverage to 0.5
  1. Preprocesssing settings
  • Switch low-pass temporal filter to OFF

Remove confounds for 5 pipelines

  1. Click on Check and run in the top navigation bar, and go to the next section.

Check and Run

  1. Click on Refresh.

You will see the spec.json file that contain all the settings and parameters you have selected.

Editing you settings

If you make changes to the settings or selected features, always click Refresh before saving and running the pipeline.

  1. Click on save.

  2. Click on Run.

  • On HPC
  • On a local machine

HALFpipe will generate files that you need to run by submitting jobs on your cluster. Wait for the green confirmation message indicating that the cluster submission script templates have been created

You can then see how to run HALFpipe on HPC

If you are running this on a local computer, the pipeline will have started. Once it has finished, continue to check your preprocessing.
